Solitary wave simulations of the Boussinesq Systems

Ozlem Ersoy, ††thanks: Ozlem Ersoy, Telephone: +90 222 2393750, Fax: +90 222 2393578, E-mail:ozersoy@ogu.edu.tr Affiliation: Department of Mathematics-Computer, Eskişehir Osmangazi University, 26480, Eskişehir, Turkey.    Idiris Dağ Affiliation: Department of Mathematics-Computer, Eskişehir Osmangazi University, 26480, Eskişehir, Turkey.    Alper Korkmaz Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Çankırı Karatekin University, 18200, Çankırı, Turkey.
Abstract

In the study, the collocation method based on exponential cubic B-spline functions is proposed to solve one dimensional Boussinesq systems numerically. Two initial boundary value problems for Regularized and Classical Boussinesq systems modeling motion of traveling waves are considered. The accuracy of the method is validated by measuring the error between the numerical and analytical solutions. The numerical solutions obtained by various values of free parameter pp are compared with some solutions in literature.

Keywords: Boussinesq sytems; solitary waves; exponential cubic B-spline; collocation.

MSC2010:  35Q99;35C07;76B25;65D07;65M70.

1 Boussinesq Systems

In the light of the d’ Alembert solution, describing two distinct waves moving in the opposite directions for the Cauchy problem for one dimensional wave equation, many physical problems modeled by linear and nonlinear partial differential equations have been solved in wave forms covering traveling waves, solitary waves, harmonic waves, etc. Waves are an important solution class for the model problems in physics, chemistry, and many fields of engineering. This solution type is widely constructed for different models in various media covering solids and fluids. Class of surface bell-shaped solitary waves, having long amplitude when compared with its width, is one of the most prominent classes of waves. In addition to linear equations, solitary wave solutions have also been studied for well known nonlinear equations and systems such as Korteweg-deVries(KdV), Schrödinger, Boussinesq, etc. Having analytical solutions only for some particular cases including additional restrictions and conditions, many numerical methods have been developed to obtain solutions for nonlinear problems.

Dougalis et al.[1] studied the numerical behavior of solitary waves of a member of Boussinesq systems family (Bona-Smith system). In that study, long time stability and possible blow-up solutions were examined under small and large perturbations covering perturbation of amplitudes, system coefficients, etc. Numerical models were constructed with the Galerkin-finite element method on the space ShS_{h} of smooth, periodic, cubic splines.

Quintic B-spline collocation tecnique based on Crank-Nicolson formulation was set up for numerical solutions of Boussines type coupled-BBM system[2]. Two initial boundary value problems describing motion of single solitary wave and interaction of solitary waves were simulated by the proposed method. The numerical results were compared with the analytical ones.

The Galerkin-finite element periodic B-spline method was used to approximate the cnoidal and solitary wave solutions of periodic initial value problem for four variable Boussinesq system[3].

In the study[4], variations of Boussinesq system, namely coupled Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) systems in Hamiltonian form, were integrated using the energy preserving average vector field scheme. The travelling waves for the KdV-KdV systems were also studied numerically by Bona et al. using unconditionally stable periodic splines Galerkin method with Gauss-Legendre implicit Runge-Kutta method of stage two[5].

Antonopoulos et al. simulated the numerical solutions of three initial boundary value problems one parameter Bona-Smith systems[6]. The problems with homogenous Dirichlet, reflection, and periodic boundary conditions were integrated by Galerkin-finite element combined with fourth order explicit Runge-Kutta method.

A meshless radial basis collocation algorithm was set up to simulate nonlinear dispersive waves propagating in two ways of Boussinesq system by Suárez and Morales[7]. The solutions for three initial boundary value problems modeling motion of single solitary and interaction of solitary waves were demonstrated with the proposed method.

Aksoy presented Taylor-Collocation extended cubic B-spline methods for the numerical solutions of the Boussinesq systems[19]. The initial boundary value problems modeling motion of single solitary waves were investigated by using various free parameters in extended cubic B-spline functions.

In this study, the authors investigate the numerical solutions for two particular initial boundary value problems for the Classical Boussinesq System (CBS) and the Regularized Boussinesq System (RBS). A collocation method based on exponential cubic B-spline functions is constructed to obtain the numerical solutions for both systems. The details of both problems and numerical methodology will be explained in the following sections.

Consider the Boussinesq system modeling bi-directional propagation of nonlinear dispersive long surface waves with small amplitudes in a channel of the form

Vt+Ux+(V​U)x+s1​Ux​x​x−s2​Vx​x​t\displaystyle V_{t}+U_{x}+(VU)_{x}+s_{1}U_{xxx}-s_{2}V_{xxt} =0\displaystyle=0 (1)
Ut+Vx+U​Ux+s3​Vx​x​x−s4​Ux​x​t\displaystyle U_{t}+V_{x}+UU_{x}+s_{3}V_{xxx}-s_{4}U_{xxt} =0\displaystyle=0

where xx denotes the distance along the channel scaled by still water of depth h0h_{0} and tt is the time scaled by h0g\sqrt{\frac{h_{0}}{g}}, with the gravitational acceleration gg[8, 9]. In order to equalize the order of the effects of both nonlinearity and dispersion, the Stokes number S=s1​λ2/h03S=s_{1}\lambda^{2}/h^{3}_{0} is assumed of order one with the small maximum deviation of surface s1s_{1} relative to h0h_{0} and λ>h0\lambda>h_{0}. In the model (1), V⁡(x,t)V(x,t) is the scaled, dimensionless deviation of the water surface, U⁡(x,t)U(x,t) is the scaled, dimensionless horizontal velocity of height θ​h0\theta h_{0}, θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1] above the bottom of the channel[9]. In the system (1), the real constants s1,s2,s3s_{1},s_{2},s_{3} and s4s_{4} are defined by;

s1\displaystyle s_{1} =12​(θ2−13)​λ\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(\theta^{2}-\frac{1}{3})\lambda (2)
s2\displaystyle s_{2} =12​(θ2−13)​(1−λ)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(\theta^{2}-\frac{1}{3})(1-\lambda)
s3\displaystyle s_{3} =12​(1−θ2)​μ\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(1-\theta^{2})\mu
s4\displaystyle s_{4} =12​(1−θ2)​(1−μ)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(1-\theta^{2})(1-\mu)

where λ\lambda and μ\mu are real[8, 10, 11].
Particular choice of the parameters θ2=13,μ=0\theta^{2}=\frac{1}{3},\mu=0 and arbitrary λ\lambda generates the CBS from the system (1)[12, 10, 9] as;

Vt+Ux+(V​U)x=0\displaystyle V_{t}+U_{x}+(VU)_{x}=0 (3)
Ut+Vx+U​Ux−13​Ux​x​t=0\displaystyle U_{t}+V_{x}+UU_{x}-\frac{1}{3}U_{xxt}=0

When the parameters are chosen as θ2=23,λ=0,μ=0\theta^{2}=\frac{2}{3},\lambda=0,\mu=0, the Boussinesq system (1) reduces to the RBS of the form [11];

Vt+Ux+(V​U)x−16​Vx​x​t\displaystyle V_{t}+U_{x}+(VU)_{x}-\frac{1}{6}V_{xxt} =0\displaystyle=0 (4)
Ut+Vx+U​Ux−16​Ux​x​t\displaystyle U_{t}+V_{x}+UU_{x}-\frac{1}{6}U_{xxt} =0\displaystyle=0

2 Exponential Cubic B-spline Collocation Method(ECC)

Let π\pi be a uniformly distributed grids of the finite interval [a,b][a,b], such as,

π:xm=a+mh,m=0,1,…N\pi:x_{m}=a+mh,m=0,1,\ldots N

where h=b−aNh=\frac{b-a}{N}. Then, the exponential cubic B-splines are defined as;

Bm​(x)={b2​((xm−2−x)−1ζ​sinh⁡(ζ⁡(xm−2−x))),[xm−2,xm−1]a1+b1​(xm−x)+c1​exp⁡(ζ⁡(xm−x))+d1​exp⁡(−ζ⁡(xm−x)),[xm−1,xm]a1+b1​(x−xm)+c1​exp⁡(ζ⁡(x−xm))+d1​exp⁡(−ζ⁡(x−xm)),[xm,xm+1]b2​((x−xm+2)−1ζ​sinh⁡(ζ⁡(x−xm+2))),[xm+1,xm+2]0,o​t​h​e​r​w​i​s​eB_{m}(x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcc}b_{2}\left((x_{m-2}-x)-\frac{1}{\zeta}\sinh(\zeta(x_{m-2}-x))\right)&,&[x_{m-2},x_{m-1}]\\ a_{1}+b_{1}(x_{m}-x)+c_{1}\exp(\zeta(x_{m}-x))+d_{1}\exp(-\zeta(x_{m}-x))&,&[x_{m-1},x_{m}]\\ a_{1}+b_{1}(x-x_{m})+c_{1}\exp(\zeta(x-x_{m}))+d_{1}\exp(-\zeta(x-x_{m}))&,&[x_{m},x_{m+1}]\\ b_{2}\left((x-x_{m+2})-\frac{1}{\zeta}\sinh(\zeta(x-x_{m+2}))\right)&,&[x_{m+1},x_{m+2}]\\ 0&,&otherwise\end{array}\right. (7)

where

a1=ζ​h​cosh⁡(ζ​h)ζ​h​cosh⁡(ζ​h)−sinh⁡(ζ​h),b1=ζ2​cosh⁡(ζ​h)​(cosh⁡(ζ​h)−1)+sinh2⁡(ζ​h)(ζ​h​cosh⁡(ζ​h)−sinh⁡(ζ​h))​(1−cosh⁡(ζ​h)),b2=ζ2​(ζ​h​cosh⁡(ζ​h)−sinh⁡(ζ​h)),c1=14​OPENexp⁡(−ζ​h)​(1−cosh⁡(ζ​h))+sinh⁡(ζ​h)​(exp⁡(−ζ​h)−1))(ζ​h​cosh⁡(ζ​h)−sinh⁡(ζ​h))​(1−cosh⁡(ζ​h)),d1=14​OPENexp⁡(ζ​h)​(cosh⁡(ζ​h)−1)+sinh⁡(ζ​h)​(exp⁡(ζ​h)−1))(ζ​h​cosh⁡(ζ​h)−sinh⁡(ζ​h))​(1−cosh⁡(ζ​h)),\begin{array}[]{l}a_{1}=\dfrac{\zeta h\cosh(\zeta h)}{\zeta h\cosh(\zeta h)-\sinh(\zeta h)},\\ b_{1}=\dfrac{\zeta}{2}\dfrac{\cosh(\zeta h)(\cosh(\zeta h)-1)+\sinh^{2}(\zeta h)}{(\zeta h\cosh(\zeta h)-\sinh(\zeta h))(1-\cosh(\zeta h))},\\ b_{2}=\dfrac{\zeta}{2(\zeta h\cosh(\zeta h)-\sinh(\zeta h))},\\ c_{1}=\dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{\exp(-\zeta h)(1-\cosh(\zeta h))+\sinh(\zeta h)(\exp(-\zeta h)-1))}{(\zeta h\cosh(\zeta h)-\sinh(\zeta h))(1-\cosh(\zeta h))},\\ d_{1}=\dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{\exp(\zeta h)(\cosh(\zeta h)-1)+\sinh(\zeta h)(\exp(\zeta h)-1))}{(\zeta h\cosh(\zeta h)-\sinh(\zeta h))(1-\cosh(\zeta h))},\end{array}

where ζ\zeta is a real parameter[14]. Each exponential cubic B-spline Bm​(x)B_{m}(x) has two continuous principle derivatives defined in the interval [xm−1,xm+2][x_{m-1},x_{m+2}] and Bm​(x)B_{m}(x) itself and its two principle derivatives vanish out of this interval. The set {B−1​(x),B0​(x),…,BN+1​(x)}\{B_{-1}(x),B_{0}(x),...,B_{N+1}(x)\} constitutes a basis for the functions defined over the interval [a,b][a,b]. Since introduced by McCartin, exponential cubic B-spline functions have been used to solve some engineering and physics problems numerically [15, 16, 17].

U⁡(x,t)≅∑m=−1N+1δm​Bm​(x)U(x,t)\cong\sum_{m=-1}^{N+1}\delta_{m}B_{m}(x) (8a)
V⁡(x,t)≅∑m=−1N+1ϕm​Bm​(x)V(x,t)\cong\sum_{m=-1}^{N+1}\phi_{m}B_{m}(x) (8b)

6 Numerical Examples

The accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method will be validated by solving initial boundary value problems for RBS and CBS. The numerical results will be compared with the analytical solutions and the Aksoy’ s numerical solutions obtained by extended cubic B-spline collocation method (EXCC) with free parameter λ\lambda[19]. The error between the numerical solution ψn​u​m\psi^{num} and the analytical solution ψa​n​a\psi^{ana} at a time tt will be measured by using discrete maximum error norm L∞​(ψ)L_{\infty}(\psi) defined as;

L∞​(ψ)=|ψa​n​a−ψn​u​m|∞=maxm⁡|ψma​n​a−ψmn​u​m|\begin{array}[]{c}L_{\infty}(\psi)=\left|\psi^{ana}-\psi^{num}\right|_{\infty}=\max\limits_{m}\left|\psi^{ana}_{m}-\psi^{num}_{m}\right|\\ \end{array}

6.1 Regularized Boussinesq System

The analytical solution for the RBS is of the form;

V⁡(x,t)\displaystyle V(x,t) =−1\displaystyle=-1
U⁡(x,t)\displaystyle U(x,t) =(1−ρ6)​Cs+Cs​ρ2​sech2⁡(ρ2​(x+x0−Cs​t))\displaystyle=(1-\dfrac{\rho}{6})C_{s}+\dfrac{C_{s}\rho}{2}\sech^{2}(\dfrac{\sqrt{\rho}}{2}(x+x_{0}-C_{s}t))

where x0x_{0} and CsC_{s} real, ρ\rho nonnegative constant[9]. This solution represents a traveling wave, the peak of which is located at x0x_{0} initially, moving along the horizontal axis with velocity CsC_{s}. The initial-boundary value problem for the RBS is constructed by combining the initial conditions

V⁡(x,0)\displaystyle V(x,0) =−1\displaystyle=-1 (18)
U⁡(x,0)\displaystyle U(x,0) =sech2⁡(62​x)\displaystyle=\sech^{2}(\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{2}x)

and the homogenous Neumann boundary conditions

∂U⁡(x,t)∂x|x=−20\displaystyle\left.\dfrac{\partial U(x,t)}{\partial x}\right|_{x=-20} =0,\displaystyle=0,\, ∂U⁡(x,t)∂x|x=30=0\displaystyle\left.\dfrac{\partial U(x,t)}{\partial x}\right|_{x=30}=0
∂V⁡(x,t)∂x|x=−20\displaystyle\left.\dfrac{\partial V(x,t)}{\partial x}\right|_{x=-20} =0,\displaystyle=0,\, ∂V⁡(x,t)∂x|x=30=0\displaystyle\left.\dfrac{\partial V(x,t)}{\partial x}\right|_{x=30}=0

over the finite interval [−20,30][-20,30]. The initial condition representing a pulse of amplitude 11 is derived from the analytical solution by a particular choice of x0=0x_{0}=0, ρ=6\rho=6 and Cs=1/3C_{s}=1/3 at the initial time t=0t=0. The numerical simulation of wave motion along the horizontal axis is accomplished with the parameters N=1000N=1000, Δ​t=0.005\Delta t=0.005 and ζ=0.0000058339\zeta=0.0000058339 up to the terminating time 1515, Fig 1. The peak of the initial pulse moves from its initial location x0=0x_{0}=0 with a constant velocity Cs=1/3C_{s}=1/3. At the terminating time t=15t=15, the peak reaches x=5x=5 without changing its shape.

For the sake of comparison with Aksoy’s work, the designed algorithms are run with fixed number grids N=1000N=1000, the various parameters ζ\zeta and and time step lengths. The measured maximum errors for both U⁡(x,t)U(x,t) and V⁡(x,t)V(x,t) at the terminating time t=5t=5 are depicted in Fig 2(a) and Fig 2(b). Even though the maximum error for U⁡(x,5)U(x,5) is located about the peak, the maximum error for V⁡(x,5)V(x,5) is about x=−15x=-15.

When ECC is compared with EXCC, one see that ECC generates a little bit better numerical results for both various choices of free parameters. When Δ​t=0.005\Delta t=0.005, the maximum error is approximately 2×10−112\times 10^{-11} for λ=0\lambda=0 and 3×10−113\times 10^{-11} for λ=−0.00297\lambda=-0.00297 for the function V⁡(x,t)V(x,t) in EXCC. Usage of the same parameters except λ\lambda, the maximum error is measured less than 10−1110^{-11} for various choices of ζ\zeta in ECC. For the function U⁡(x,t)U(x,t), the accuracy of the numerical results are in the same digits for both methods for various values of free parameters λ\lambda and ζ\zeta.

6.2 Classical Boussinesq System (CBS)

The traveling wave solution for CBS is,

V⁡(x,t)\displaystyle V(x,t) =−1\displaystyle=-1
U⁡(x,t)\displaystyle U(x,t) =(1−ρ3)​Cs+Cs​ρ2​sech2⁡(ρ2​(x+x0−Cs​t))\displaystyle=(1-\dfrac{\rho}{3})C_{s}+\dfrac{C_{s}\rho}{2}\sech^{2}(\dfrac{\sqrt{\rho}}{2}(x+x_{0}-C_{s}t))

where x0x_{0} and CsC_{s} are real, ρ\rho is non negative constants[9]. This solution represents a traveling wave along the horizontal axis with velocity CsC_{s} as time goes. The initial boundary value problem for CBS is constructed by combining the initial condition

V⁡(x,0)\displaystyle V(x,0) =−1\displaystyle=-1
U⁡(x,0)\displaystyle U(x,0) =sech2⁡(32​x)\displaystyle=\sech^{2}(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}x)

which is generated by a particular choice of the constants as x0=0x_{0}=0, ρ=3\rho=3 and Cs=1/3C_{s}=1/3 at the initial time t=0t=0 in the analytical solution, and the homogenous Neumann boundary conditions covering only first order derivatives at both ends. By those selection of parameters, the analytical solution representing a traveling wave of amplitude 11 and of initial peak position 00 moves along the horizontal axis with velocity 1/31/3 as time goes. The simulation of the numerical solution is depicted with N=1000N=1000, Δ​t=0.005\Delta t=0.005 and ζ=0.0000086530\zeta=0.0000086530 up to the terminating time t=15t=15, Fig 3. The initial pulse moves along the horizontal axis without changing its shape during the simulation. The peak position becomes x=t×Cs=15×13=5x=t\times C_{s}=15\times\frac{1}{3}=5 at the terminating time t=15t=15. The error distribution for both function are graphed with the parameters N=1000N=1000, Δ​t=0.005\Delta t=0.005 and ζ=0.0000086530\zeta=0.0000086530 at the time t=5t=5 in Fig 4(a)-4(b). The maximum errors are measured about 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} for U⁡(x,5)U(x,5) and 1×10−141\times 10^{-14} for V⁡(x,5)V(x,5).

The results are compared with the analytical solutions and Aksoy’ s solutions by measuring the error between numerical and analytical solutions for various values of the parameter ζ\zeta, Table 3- Table 4. Even though the accuracy of V⁡(x,t)V(x,t) are almost the same in both methods, the accuracy of U⁡(x,t)U(x,t) appears a little bit better for various values of free parameters in ECC.

7 Conclusion

In the study, the exponential cubic B-spline collocation algorithm is designed to solve two initial boundary value problems modeling traveling wave solutions for Regularized Boussinesq and Classical Boussinesq systems. The equations in systems are discretized in time by Crank-Nicolson and finite difference methods. Then, the resultant equations are discretized in space by collocation method based on exponential B-splines. The simulations are obtained successfully by the proposed method.
The error of numerical results is measured using discrete maximum error norm and compared with the results obtained by Aksoy’s method based on extended cubic B-splines. The comparison shows that the results obtained by the proposed method in this study generate more accurate results than Aksoy’s results for some problems due to the appropriate choice of free parameter ζ\zeta. For the remaining problems, the results are acceptable and as accurate as Aksoy’s results.
